# The Hateful Immortals

## A Documentary Record of the Greenbriar-Chen Marriage (1849–2024), Compiled and Annotated by Dr. Eleanor Thornton, Department of Parahistorical Studies, University of Michigan

---

### Editor's Note

*The following document was assembled over a period of nine years from primary sources including personal correspondence, municipal records, daguerreotypes, immigration paperwork, lease agreements, three partially burned journals, one fully burned journal (recovered via spectrographic reconstruction), and approximately 340 hours of recorded interviews conducted between 2019 and 2024. Unless otherwise noted, all quotations attributed to Margaret Greenbriar-Chen are drawn from her own oral testimony and should be understood as verbatim reproductions of the original exchanges, per the well-documented nature of her condition. Quotations attributed to James Greenbriar-Chen are, by his own cheerful admission, "more or less in the neighborhood." —E.T.*

---

### I. Origins, Courtship, and the Vow

Margaret Fenn was thirteen years old, seated in the fifth pew of the Second Congregational Church of Braintree, Massachusetts, on the morning of October 11, 1840, when the Reverend Dr. Josiah Hallett delivered a sermon on the Book of Ruth lasting approximately forty-five minutes.[^1] The following Sunday, she approached the reverend after the service and recited the entire address back to him, pausing twice—once to note that he had misattributed a secondary quotation to Chrysostom when it belonged to Ambrose, and once to observe that his exegesis of Ruth 1:16 had "elided the conditional grammar of the Hebrew in a manner that, while perhaps liturgically convenient, was not, strictly speaking, accurate."[^2]

She was not, by her own account, trying to correct him. She simply remembered it—all of it, every word, every pause, the particular wheeze in his breathing when he reached the top of a rhetorical crescendo—and she had spent the intervening week with it sitting in her mind like a piece of furniture she had not ordered and could not return, and she wanted someone else to take it back.

No one could. No one ever would. That was the nature of the thing.

The medical and parahistorical literature on eidetic totality is, at this point, extensive,[^3] and I will not rehearse it here except to note what the clinical descriptions invariably fail to convey: it is not merely that Margaret Greenbriar-Chen remembers everything. It is that she remembers everything *at its original fidelity and emotional temperature*. A slight delivered in 1897 does not, as it would for the rest of us, undergo the merciful processes of compression, distortion, and eventual softening that cognitive science calls "reconsolidation" and that ordinary people call "getting over it." It sits in her memory at full volume, full color, full sting, as retrievable in 2024 as it was in the moment of its infliction. She does not carry a grudge. She carries the event itself, perfectly preserved, and the grudge is simply what it feels like to hold a thing that never decays.

James Chen was fifteen, the son of a Cantonese merchant and a Scottish dockworker's daughter in the Broad Street ward of Boston,[^4] when, on a Tuesday afternoon in March of 1842, a dray horse startled at a fire bell and kicked him squarely in the left temple with sufficient force to, in the words of the attending physician, "stave in the lateral aspect of the cranium to a depth inconsistent with the continuation of life."[^5]

James sat back up. He was, by several witness accounts, annoyed.

The physician, a Dr. Edwin Greer, noted in his casebook that the boy's skull appeared to "reconstitute itself over a period of some eight to ten minutes, during which the patient complained primarily of the interruption to his afternoon and secondarily of a headache he described as 'middling.'"[^6] Dr. Greer subsequently tested the limits of this apparent regenerative capacity by means I will not catalogue here, as they would constitute, by modern standards, a war crime. James survived all of them. He appears to have found most of them boring.

The two met five years later, at the Boston Lyceum's 1847 lecture series on phrenology and the moral sciences—an event Margaret can still narrate in its entirety, including the audience's coughing patterns and the specific squeak of the lecturer's left shoe, and that James recalls as "some kind of talk, I think, about heads."[^7]

The courtship lasted two years. It was conducted, as courtships of the period were, through supervised visits, carefully composed letters, and the elaborate social choreography of mid-century New England propriety—all of which Margaret can reproduce, down to the weather on each occasion, and all of which James remembers as a general sense of warmth, admiration, and "Margaret being very lively and smelling like soap, good soap, the kind with lavender."[^8]

That this asymmetry did not prevent the development of genuine attachment is evident from the letters themselves, which survive in their entirety because Margaret's memory constitutes, in effect, a second and incorruptible archive. James's letters to Margaret—the physical copies of which were lost in a San Francisco fire in 1906 and a Buenos Aires flood in 1938—are preserved in her recollection with what I have been able to verify, by cross-reference with the six surviving originals, as absolute accuracy.[^9] They are, I should note, better than one might expect. He had a plainspoken tenderness that the era's conventions could not entirely bury. "I am not a learned man," he wrote on April 3, 1848, "and I cannot dress my thoughts in Sunday clothes the way you do, but I will tell you what I have, which is that I think about you when you are not in the room, and the room is worse for it, and I am worse for it, and I would like to solve this by being in whatever room you are in for as long as you'll have me, and if that is a small ambition for a man, then I am a small man and happy to be one."[^10]

Margaret, when she recited this letter to me, did so in a tone I can only describe as prosecutorial—as though presenting evidence of a crime she had not yet named.

They were married on June 14, 1849, at the Second Congregational Church of Braintree, by a new minister who had replaced the Reverend Hallett and who was, Margaret notes, "a less careful reader of Ambrose."

The vows were standard for the period's Episcopal-influenced Congregationalist liturgy. I reproduce them here in full, as Margaret delivered them from memory during our first interview, because they constitute, for the purposes of this document, not merely a personal commitment but a structural condition—the foundational clause of a contract that both parties would spend the next 177 years attempting to interpret:

> *Minister: Will you have this man to be your husband; to live together in the covenant of marriage? Will you love him, comfort him, honor and keep him, in sickness and in health; and, forsaking all others, be faithful to him as long as you both shall live?*
>
> *Margaret: I will.*
>
> *Minister: Will you have this woman to be your wife; to live together in the covenant of marriage? Will you love her, comfort her, honor and keep her, in sickness and in health; and, forsaking all others, be faithful to her as long as you both shall live?*
>
> *James: I will.*
>
> *Minister: Those whom God has joined together, let no one put asunder. Until death do you part.*

The phrase is, of course, traditional. In the overwhelmingly common case, it functions as an earnest if somewhat melodramatic way of saying "for a very long time"—the upper bound being, for the couples of 1849, perhaps fifty years, with actuarial reality tending to intervene well before that. For a woman who would remember every moment of the marriage at full fidelity and a man whom death would simply decline to collect, the phrase constitutes not a promise but a null clause: a condition that, by the specific terms of their respective conditions, can never be satisfied, and therefore can never release either party from the obligations it governs.[^11]

They were, by all available evidence, very happy on their wedding day. Margaret describes James's expression during the vows as "solemn and glad in equal measure, and his left hand trembled slightly, and he wore a cravat I had not seen before, dark blue, with a small stain near the bottom that I believe was coffee."[^12]

James, asked for his recollection of the ceremony, said: "Oh, she was beautiful. She's always been beautiful. I cried, I think. Or maybe she did. One of us did."

---

The first marital argument preserved in the documentary record occurred in March of 1852, in the two-room apartment on Myrtle Street in Boston where they had spent the first three years of their marriage, and concerned a window.

Specifically: whether James had left the bedroom window open overnight on the evening of March 7th, admitting a quantity of cold air and (Margaret believed) a bat.

Margaret's account, delivered to me 172 years later with an eerie, metronomic precision that I have come to recognize as the particular cadence she adopts when reciting testimony she considers damning:

> *Margaret: I said to him, "James, you have left the window open again, and the room is absolutely frigid, and I am nearly certain something flew in." And he said, "I don't think I left it open." And I said, "You did, because I heard you get up at half past eleven, and I heard the latch, and the draft began at that exact moment, and there is a bat." And he said—and I want to be precise here—he said, "Maggie, you may have heard a sound, but I don't recall getting up." And I said, "You don't recall it because you don't recall anything. I recall it because I recall everything. The window was opened at half past eleven, the draft entered from the north-northwest, and there is a bat in the curtain." And he said, "Well, if there's a bat in the curtain, I'll get the bat." And he got the bat. But he never admitted to the window.*

James's account, delivered in 2024:

> *James: There may have been a window situation at some point. I don't recall the specifics.*

The asymmetry here is, I think, self-evident, but it warrants explicit articulation because it would prove structural. In the Greenbriar-Chen marriage, one party possesses a complete, unimpeachable, emotionally undiminished record of every exchange, and the other party possesses goodwill, a cheerful vagueness, and the serene confidence of a man who has been kicked in the skull by a horse, shot, stabbed, burned, drowned, and hit by two separate automobiles in two separate centuries and has found all of these experiences to be, at worst, temporarily inconvenient. Margaret cannot forget a grievance. James cannot be permanently harmed by one. She accumulates; he regenerates. Every wound she catalogues is eternal; every wound he sustains is passing. They are, in this sense, perfectly mismatched—each one's defining trait rendering the other's either moot or maddening, depending on the century, the argument, and the prevailing cultural consensus on whether a marriage such as theirs should be described as "enduring" or "entrenched." Over the course of 177 years, every consensus has been tried. None has fit.

---

### II. The Special Places

One of the more logistically demanding aspects of the Greenbriar-Chen marriage—and one that the existing parahistorical literature tends to treat as a footnote rather than as the perpetual, grinding, low-grade catastrophe both parties describe it as—is the matter of relocation.

People notice when their neighbors don't age. They notice slowly in some eras and quickly in others; they notice sooner in small communities and later in large cities; they notice with suspicion in some centuries and with polite, determined obliviousness in others. But they notice. Margaret estimates that the outer limit, in any given location, is approximately fifteen to twenty years before the questions become unmanageable. James estimates "ten, maybe? somewhere in there." They have, by Margaret's count, maintained primary residences in seventeen different cities across nine countries.[^13] Each of these locations is stored in Margaret's memory at full resolution—every room, every neighbor, every meal, every argument—and it is this completeness, rather than the frequency of the moves, that constitutes what I have come to understand as one of the marriage's central and least visible cruelties.

Normal people romanticize the places they've left. Memory softens the apartment where you were poor; it films over the neighbors who were awful; it gradually replaces the real experience with a warmer, vaguer, more bearable version. Margaret Greenbriar-Chen cannot do this. She cannot soften Myrtle Street or gild Buenos Aires or blur Portland. She carries every place as it actually was—the happiness unsweetened, the misery undiminished, the ordinary days preserved in all their ordinary, irreducible texture—and this means that she can never grieve a home in the way grieving requires, which is to say, inaccurately.

James, by contrast, grieves each departure for approximately one and a half days and then begins researching the next city with what Margaret describes as "an enthusiasm verging on the indecent."

I will not attempt to document all seventeen residences. What follows is a representative selection, chosen for the clarity with which each illustrates the operative dynamics of the marriage and, I acknowledge, for reasons of narrative economy.[^14]

---

**Paris, 1871–1889**

They arrived in the autumn of 1871, five months after the suppression of the Commune, and took an apartment on the rue du Bac that Margaret describes in such comprehensive architectural and sensory detail that I was able, with the assistance of a graduate student and municipal records, to identify the specific building, which is now a mobile phone retailer.[^15]

The Paris years are characterized in Margaret's account by two parallel and coextensive realities. The first is domestic: a detailed, unsparing catalogue of James's habits in the apartment, including but not limited to his persistent placement of his boots on the settee ("a Louis XV reproduction with a silk damask cover that I had sourced with considerable effort from a shop on the rue Jacob, and he treated it as a boot rack, Eleanor, a *boot rack*"), his failure to properly trim candlewicks, his tendency to sing Cantonese folk songs slightly off-key while shaving, and his habit of returning from errands with items they had not discussed and did not need, such as the occasion in April of 1879 when he returned from the boulangerie with a small and, Margaret maintains, "structurally unsound" writing desk that he had purchased from a street vendor because "it looked lonely."

Margaret catalogued the boot infractions. There were, by her count, 1,437 instances of boots on the settee between 1871 and 1889. She acknowledges that this figure may contain a margin of error of one or two instances, not because her memory is imprecise but because on a handful of occasions James placed only *one* boot on the settee while wearing the other, and she is uncertain whether these should be counted as full or partial infractions. She has, in 153 years, not resolved this methodological question.

The second reality is the one James inhabits: broader, less precise, more concerned with weather and food and the general emotional temperature of a room. His account of the Paris years centers on a single afternoon during the final days of the Commune, May 1873—a date Margaret immediately corrects to "May 24, 1871, which was the Commune, James, 1873 was nothing"—when, with fighting in the streets to the north and fires visible from their windows, he walked out of the apartment and returned ninety minutes later carrying a still-warm baguette from the boulangerie Poilâne on the rue du Cherche-Midi, which was Margaret's favorite.

Margaret does not dispute this. She remembers the baguette. She remembers the precise moment he returned—the time (4:47 p.m.), the expression on his face ("idiotic and pleased"), the smear of ash on his left shoulder, the warmth of the bread when he placed it in her hands. She also remembers that he had been shot twice during the errand—once in the abdomen and once in the upper left arm—based on the holes in his waistcoat, which she examined after he fell asleep, and which he never mentioned.

When I asked James about the gunshot wounds, he said, "Did I? Probably. That was a messy week."

When I asked Margaret what she did with the bread, she said: "I ate it. It was good bread."
